title: The Batman and Batman v Superman are proof that referencing other acclaimed works of art doesn't necesarrily improve you film(and can even be detrimental).

commenti.body:
The Falcone-Selina relationship is far more likely a reference to the Loeb/Sale graphic novels that serve as narrative basis for the whole film (The Long Halloween/Dark Victory). In those books, Selina is Carmine's illegitimate daughter. It's not a random Chinatown shoe-horn. It's an adaptation of actual source material. 

Also, I disagree that it detracts from the weight of Annika's role in the story. Earlier in the film, Selina intimates that her mother was murdered via strangulation, but doesn't say who by, just that Carmine abandoned and neglected her after that. 

She originally plans to rob him and make off with the money because she has no love for him (the score is why she's working at the Iceberg lounge), but Annika's murder throws a wrench into that and solving it becomes her priority. As the mystery unfolds, she discovers that Carmine killed Annika by...strangling her. With the pieces put together, her disdain becomes murderous, vengeful rage for obvious reasons and the trauma of her mother's murder rises to the surface again, with Annika as the important catalyst for it.
Great reply.

> The Falcone-Selina relationship is far more likely a reference to the Loeb/Sale graphic novels that serve as narrative basis for the whole film (The Long Halloween/Dark Victory). In those books, Selina is Carmine's illegitimate daughter. It's not a random Chinatown shoe-horn. It's an adaptation of actual source material.


Uhh...Matt Reeves himself confirmed The Chinatown inspiration.

> “[The dynamic is] sort of this mix of Klute with Chinatown,” says Reeves. “Because in Chinatown, I think the Evelyn Mulwray character [played by Faye Dunaway] is a classic femme fatale, but as you get deeper into the story, [Jack Nicholson] assumes that she is a certain kind of person and assumes certain things about her morally, assumes she might be connected with this murder. But as he gets deeper into it, he understands the larger story and starts to realize that her story’s quite tragic and that he’s completely misjudged her.”

and

> With the pieces put together, her disdain becomes murderous, vengeful rage for obvious reasons and the trauma of her mother's murder rises to the surface again, with Annika as the important catalyst for it. "This is for my mother" is also "This is for Annika", Annika is effectively Selina's mother 20 years ago, as a result of Carmine's cycle of violence.

You're just describing the plot and then make a leap at the end. A cycle of violence implies action-retaliation resulting in a "cycle of violence". As I said, she already sets out with the assumption he most likely had her killed(either by himself or through his men). Does the difference between disdain and murderous rage really hinge on the method of execution? 

No offense, you basically described the plot in a flowery way but haven't really justified the writing in any meaningful way.

Just because he’s comparing his film to Chinatown doesn’t mean he made a purposeful choice to try and shoe horn any of the plot of Chinatown into his film, he’s just pointing out thematic similarities. Those same similarities about Chinatown and The Batman could just as easily be made to Chinatown and The Long Halloween/Dark Victory. 

I’m not saying your criticism about Selina failing to mention Annika in the climax of the film is necessarily unwarranted, but it’s not because Revees is too busy trying to pay homage to other works. It’s just because that’s the way he structured the film.

>Uhh...Matt Reeves himself confirmed The Chinatown inspiration.

Yes, The Batman was inspired by a lot of 70s noir/neo-noir, including Chinatown. The source material is still the source material though, and your quote describes how the detective-femme fatale relationship is analogous to the one in The Batman. He doesn't say implicitly or explicitly the nature of Falcone and Selina's relationship is based *entirely* on Chinatown, because it isn't. There's enough out there on the TLH inspiration as well.

>As I said, she already sets out with the assumption he most likely had her killed(either by himself or through his men). Does the difference between disdain and murderous rage really hinge on the method of execution? 

If it wasn't clear before, you're operating on a wrong assumption. In the scene with Batman on the roof, she explicitly states that her mother was strangled and I quote *"she never found out who. Probably some creep from the club"*. So no, she doesn't know or think Carmine killed her mom until he does the same thing to Annika. Her original beef is Carmine's neglect: *"social services came to take me away, and he didn't say a thing"*. This is not even subtext, just actual text from the scene. Rewatch it yourself.

Finding out that Carmine did Annika himself and that his preferred method of femicide is strangulation is when she figures out that he also directly killed her mom. Hence my "flowery language", etc. From disdain to murderous rage.

This reads like someone who wanted to dislike The Batman for some reason and found basically nothing so came up with nonsense instead, just a willful misreading of the movie and the story that's happening, and of what Reeves was saying.

> He doesn't say implicitly or explicitly the nature of Falcone and Selina's relationship is based entirely on Chinatown, because it isn't

He's very much saying it implicitily, he's not saying it explicitly because it's supposed to be a twist in the film. Of course, he's not going to come out and explain that in the interview.

> with Batman on the roof, she explicitly states that her mother was strangled and I quote she "never found out who. Probably some creep from the club". So no, she doesn't know or think Carmine killed her mom until he does the same thing to Annika. 

I think you're the one misunderstanding things here. I'm referring to Annika in that quote not her mom. My point is her kidnapping and her considering the very likely possibilty of her friends death should be enough for anger. Knowing he killed her mother and then Annika died the same way isn't really needed. Whether she starts out knowing her mom was killed by Falcone from the beginning or not isn't the issue here. The point is there's no need to have both, either one would've sufficed.

> Hence my "flowery language", etc.

You're trying to create a narrative tissue where one didn't exist. I mean this.

>  "This is for my mother" is also "This is for Annika".

Just sounded silly.

> Just because he’s comparing his film to Chinatown doesn’t mean he made a purposeful choice to try and shoe horn any of the plot of Chinatown into his film, he’s just pointing out thematic similarities

No filmmaker is going to come outright and say it. This is as close to saying "I was inspired by it" as you can get. I find it amusing that no one is questioning the excalibur inspiration for BvS. 

> but it’s not because Revees is too busy trying to pay homage to other works. It’s just because that’s the way he structured the film.

A lot of the film's issues stems from it being a worse off version of its inspirations. I'm just saying this is another instance.

> This reads like someone who wanted to dislike The Batman for some reason

If I wanted to list reasons there's plenty. The films flaws aren't exactly not-talked about.

> nothing so came up with nonsense instead.

Right, criticising the movie for not even doing the bare minimum of even name dropping a dead character that was the prime motivation for one of our protagonists in a moment where she's about to take revenge on the guy (while name dropping another loved he killed) like you expect is...nonsense.
How do you read that beautiful analysis and throw it away like it's nothing.
Weird that you didn't list those reasons for critique at any point, and it's already explained to you why that line of critique is nonsense to anyone with even a scrap of media literacy.
You need to read more analysis if you think writing the plot summary count as one. That's all I have to say.
You need to read more analysis if you think writing the plot summary count as one. That's all I have to say.

> Weird that you didn't list those reasons for critique at any point

You need to learn to read then

> After this, even movie seems to forget about this Annika's existence because when she's about kill Falcone she just says "This is for my mother, remember her??" and Just that. Not even a "and for Annika". There's no proper conclusion or catharsis to that subplot despite it taking up a good chunk of the movie's runtime.

Lol
> that line of critique is nonsense

The user tried to handwave it by saying "The name dropping of the mother should count as one for her friend too". That's not a rebuttal, that's headcanon. 

>  scrap of media literacy.

Trying to get personal are we? You're not "media literate". Media literacy is just a phrase you use to condescend to anyone who doesn't take up your half-formed thoughts as legitimate insights. I know your ilk, you always end up defending polished turds like The Batman because it doesn't take a lot to fool you.
You don't really have a leg to stand on with that statement.
You can point to where I pretended a plot summary is "beautiful analysis". I never said that of my posts for sure. That's not even a decent analysis unless your point of reference is Jeremy Jahns.

I see this as neither proof of that nor “detrimental” to the story of the film. I do think The Batman has several well documented flaws, and sure, this might be a very minute “flaw” with the story, but I think the broader thing that you’re ignoring is how the relationship between Selina and Annika takes on new meaning with each subsequent reveal about her character. More to me, I think, is that this is really more indicative of a crucial flaw of the film, which is an uncharacteristic of the genre fidelity to a black and white morality system where Selina, as being revealed to have personal motive and selfish ideations, becomes an unambiguous good guy in the third act. This is more obvious and documented through the Gotham PD, the Wayne family, Alfred, Bruce, and on the other side Penguin, Falcone, and Riddler even.  

If, as you say, Reeves had kept to the reference of Chinatown and other neonoir, and more accurately, regular outright noir, the ending of the film would look entirely different and the mother and Annika, rather than redundancies, would be complimentary opposites to one another, with Selina being caught in the middle. 

Though as someone who liked the movie, I’m mostly fine with this specific aspect of it, so that’s why I don’t necessarily agree.
Very well written

If we remove all the Riddler/Bruce Wayne stuff the Batman becomes a pretty excellent Catwoman movie.

So you're really here telling me what I'm allowed to call a beautiful analysis or not? 

Also, I'm not the original commentor of that post, I just liked it. Still do, in blatant disregard of your lauded status as the Analysis Authority.

Annika is just a stand-in for Selina’s mother during the earlier part of the movie. The whole reason Selina even gets close with Annika is because Annika worked at the club just like her mother and Selina wants to look out for her. Both Annika and Selina’s mother are killed by Falcone strangling them, which is the big indicator that there’s a parallel between them

Selina’s story is about wanting to leave Gotham but being tied down by unanswered questions about her loved ones dying and being “owed” money from Falcone because she feels that he abandoned her as a kid

When she’s seeking justice for Annika and tracking down her kidnappers, she’s also seeking justice for mom. When she’s trying to kill Falcone to avenge her mother, she’s also trying to avenge Annika. The characters aren’t the same person but serve the same role in the story

I think if you looked at further Matt Reeves interviews (specifically where he presented the first teaser to the film), you’ll find that he also listed a ton of Batman graphic novels he pulled inspiration from. None of these pieces of art, whether it’s film or comicbooks, exist in a vacuum. They all clearly inspire one another and share thematic parallels, 

Selina being Falcone’s illegitimate child IS in the source material, and also happens to be a plot point in Chinatown. I’m sure this didn’t go unnoticed by Reeves. But I think the bigger Chinatown influence from that quote you mentioned isn’t that plot point, but rather the characters of Evelyn Mulwray and Selina Kyle both being subversions of the femme fatale. They have the appearance of someone who is dangerous and untrustworthy, but it’s just an exterior covering up the fact that they’re trying to protect a loved one.

I wouldn’t consider this a failure of a film reference. It’s just character work.

I haven't seen any of Jacques Rivettes films, but I think he had a quote that was like, "it's stupid to avoid films to avoid their influence. You choose what influenced you." Godard said "it's not where you take things from, it's where you take things too." He may have also said something like our failures to copy artists reveals our style. 

Just like anything, it can be done well or not. I haven't seen those superhero films, so I can't judge them. In Goodfellas, Scorsese winked to the audience by having Pesci shoot at them in reference to silent films. It was a cathartic way to end a harrowing movie. Even casual movie goers would understand that he was breaking the fourth wall. 

Some can find that purposely alienating, like Ebert saw the ending of The Taste of Cherry, where there's a jarring cut to the making of the film. I thought it was a challenge to question how deep our empathy runs. For maybe most of the audience, the character was half a world away.

I think that BvS moment works. It was set up earlier with the bath tub scene and the flower he gives her. The flower and spear parallel is a recurring motif throughout the movie (with Bruce as well—which could be a whole discussion to dissect). In the context of the scene itself, it seemed to heighten the stakes and led to a nice moment between Clark and Lois before he flys off with the spear.

So because he said he was inspired by Chinatown he can't possibly also have been inspired by other things, like the stories from the comics? Also her saying "this is for mom" (i don't remember the exact wording) why would this mean she simply stopped caring about her gf? Selina ofc knew Falcone was bad, but she probably didn't think that he himself had killed her mom, they had been in a relationship after all. That's obviously quite a shock after so many years, but you seem to have a strange need for Selina to also mention Annika when going for the kill of him. Very weird thing to be upset about.. Anyway you definitely lost this discussion, vs people better at  this *and* at English than me, but you should rather post this...theory(?) on the TheBatman sub. That's also a nice subred though, they don't like people getting personal as soon as someone disagrees with them any more than the people here do

He is using framing from Chinatown to tell a story that is from the comics. You can post as many Reeves comments as you want but it is a direct adaptation from source material and it’s not some coincidence he unknowingly stumbled upon. Reeves using Chinatown as a parallel for Catwoman’s subplot is no different than him using Se7en and Zodiac as inspirations for telling The Riddler’s story or using modern day social media radicalization for the third act climax.
